Madam President, The Republic of Belarus is delighted to participate in this event dedicated to the 40th anniversary of the adoption of the Declaration on the Right to Development. We reject the right of those who wield the most power to forge the world order. Fourth, it should be underpinned by the rule of law and respect for sovereignty, rather than the so-called rules-based order. a notion that is reinvented by Western countries time and time again. Good afternoon, Madam President, Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen. Today we commemorate a milestone achieved 40 years ago when we proclaimed the right to development an inalienable human right. The Kingdom of the Netherlands is a strong supporter of the reform processes that work to make the UN more representative, resilient, and effective in delivering on its mandates. Chair, India appreciates the convening of this commemorative event marking the 40th anniversary of the Declaration of the Right to Development. The world has changed over the past four decades. The declaration's promise remain unfulfilled. Debt, distrust, and financial instability deprive states of resources. The legacies of colonialism and discrimination persist in unequal access to finance, technology, and representation in international institutions. Operationalizing the right to development is an urgent imperative. India was among the earliest champions of this right. It is embedded in our philosophy, constitutional framework, and welfare architecture. Several initiatives by Government of India, together with financial inclusion and India's digital public infrastructure, have empowered individuals, households, and enterprises, helping more than 250 million Indians emerge from multidimensional poverty over the past decade. Chair, in an interconnected world, national action alone is insufficient. The declaration requires meaningful international cooperation. India's development partnerships with the Global South are demand-driven and pursued through grants, concessional lines of credit, capacity building, and humanitarian assistance. We believe that we must reform the multilateral system and international financial architecture to prevent the reversal of development gains and ensure a voice of voice for developing countries. Discussion has been confined to whether the right to development is individual or collective. We must move beyond this binary. The right belongs to individuals and peoples alike, and brings civil, political, economic, social, and cultural rights together to enable the full realization of human potential. India reiterates its support for the declaration and for the early adoption of the Covenant on the right to development. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of India. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Bangladesh.

Mr. President, Four decades ago, we reaffirmed the right to development as an inalienable right of every person and nation. Yet poverty, exclusion and inequality continue to deny millions dignity and opportunity. Climate change, debt, shrinking development, finance, protectionism, technology divides and conflicts are eroding hard-won gains and widening inequalities. The COVID-19 pandemic has further deepened these challenges. The 2030 agenda renewed our commitment to the right to development, but sustainable development cannot thrive amid inequality and exclusion. Following restoration of democracy, our government adopted a pro-people policy for social and economic development. In our journey towards transformative changes, we uphold the spirit of Vienna Declaration and Programme of Action. We are advancing our development agenda to empower every citizen through a targeted social protection initiatives including family cards, farmers cards and expanded access to free postgraduate education. We are bringing development benefits to every household. With women comprising nearly half of our population, we are committed to their full participation in development. But we are investing in our youth as partners in development. Guided by the vision of a rainbow nation, we seek to build an inclusion society where no one is left behind. Yet no nation can achieve the right to development alone. It requires shared commitment, responsibility, and action of all nations. It is now time to turn our pronouncement of declaration into action and shared prosperity. Bangladesh, therefore, proposes four priorities. First, to make global financial architecture fair, inclusive, and responsive to developing countries. Second, to deliver on development and climate finance predictably and equitably. Third, to ensure equitable access to all of all to technology and artificial intelligence and make them drivers of shared development. And finally, to adopt a legally binding framework that transforms the right to development from aspirations into accountability. I thank you all.
I thank the distinguished representative of Bangladesh. Now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Spain.

Madam President, to our excellencies, distinguished colleagues, it's a great honor for Spain to speak at this fundamental landmark. Four decades ago, the international community adopted a vision of universal justice with the human being at the very center of development policies. And although we can note that there have been vast examples of progress, if we look at where we are now, just a few years from the deadline of the Sustainable Development Agenda, we have to realize that progress has been unequal, jeopardized by successive crisis, with the structural imbalances in a system that has a legacy of asymmetries and a suffocating lack of funding. For Spain, the declaration is part of a vision that is holistic, intersectional, an inalienable right for people at the center. People drive and benefit from sustainable development and states with the responsibilities incumbent upon them have to protect, drive forward and guarantee that all human rights be ensured pursuant to the international obligations without any discrimination. We have to see that participation is not a dead letter, it's free, informed, active, so that men and women can be true decision makers. We can ensure the rights of indigenous peoples, those with disabilities, LGBT people, with no exceptions. Spain sees development as inclusive and sustainable. And we have a multidimensional, intersectional vision that requires consistent policies taking into account our citizens. We need real resources aiming at welfare and equality. When we consider our international commitments to human rights and sustainable development, we enter into commitments with promoting of women's rights, development, the right to food, because without real equality between men and women, without culture, without progress, looking at eradicating hunger, there can be no sustainable development. Following the International Conference on Development and the Seville Commitment, Spain had an opportunity to promote a new global funding contract, again looking at all the needs of our globe. The international financial architecture has to be governed by standards, ensuring real participation with adequate funding so that nobody be left behind. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Spain. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Norway.

Thank you, Madam President. I am pleased to make the Norwegian statement on the right to declare the development. I have three points to make. First, development and human rights goes hand in hand. They are not separate goals. You cannot fully achieve or sustain one without the other. Development is not charity, it is shared responsibility. We must create conditions for all people to live with dignity, realize their rights and have equal opportunities to succeed. This requires action from all of us, especially those with the greatest resources. Norway will continue to be a committed partner through political engagement, international cooperation, and with aid budget at a high level. Second, job creation is now the primary objective of Norwegian development policy. The most sustainable way out of poverty is a job. Work provides income, dignity, and opportunity. Aid remains important, but it is not enough. We must build economies that create jobs and enable countries to stand on their own over time. Norway has strengthened our tools, such as Norfund, our development finance institution, to support these efforts. We look forward to work with other partners to make it happen. Third, and my last point, gender equality. non-discrimination and inclusion are fundamental human rights principles. Recent setbacks and funding cuts are of big concern from us in Norway. We must not allow those at most risk of exclusion to be weakened. Human rights Gender equality, sexual and reproductive health and rights, and the rights of the LGBTQ+ persons must remain priorities. Norway will continue to stand up for women's rights, women's rights to decide over their own body, and human rights for all. Madam President, our message is simple. Developments must go hand in hand with human rights. create opportunities through job and ensure inclusion and dignity for all. Norway will continue to be a committed partner. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Norway. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Mali.

Madame President, ladies and gentlemen, Forty years ago, the Declaration on the Right to Development was adopted by the United Nations General Assembly. Many hopes were pinned on the Declaration by people all over the planet. The right to development is not a matter of charity, it's a matter of equity, of autonomy, and participation on the part of the majority of the world's people, Mali is unswervingly committed to implementing the 2030 agenda as well as the sustainable development goals, despite the persistent effects of a multidimensional crisis which has beset Mali for over a decade. We are less than five years away from the 2030 agenda. And for Mali, the main challenge is not just continuing SDG implementation, but substantively accelerating progress against the areas where progress is insufficient, locking in what we've achieved already. Implementing the SDGs must go beyond promises. This is why Mali has created Vision Mali Koura 2063, Implementing the national strategy for Malawi's emergence and sustainable development 2024-2033, undergoing a structural overhaul of our economy. Despite taxing conditions, we continue to exhibit resilience and SDG growth. GDP growth stood at roughly 6% in 2025. and a number of leading sectors drove growth. However, this trend is fragile given the structure of our economy, the size of the informal sector, as well as low local value added, as well as ongoing difficulties related to infrastructure, energy, hydro, and transport. The improvements we've seen on domestic resource mobilization reflects the government's ambition to progressively increase development funding out of national resources. In order to ensure everyone can live and enjoy good health and well-being, the government of Mali is continuing its efforts aimed at improving access to quality health services, in particular by making some basic health services free and improving community health clinics. As for employment, the government is trying to translate economic growth into decent, productive jobs, something that should benefit to young people and women first and foremost.

The distinguished representative of Mali. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Azerbaijan.

Excellencies, distinguished colleagues, 40 years ago, the General Assembly adopted the Declaration on the Right to Development, affirming that every person and all peoples are entitled to participate in and enjoy economic, social, and cultural, and political development. Reaffirmed in 1993 as a universal and inalienable human right, this declaration remains as relevant as ever. While significant progress has been achieved, Poverty, conflict, debt, and climate change continue to undermine development prospects for millions. Developing countries also face persistent gaps in access to finance, technology, and global markets. Development must remain at the heart of our collective efforts. Realizing this right requires national policies and enabling international environment based on solidarity, trust, and multilateralism. We must ensure that emerging technologies like artificial intelligence create opportunities for all rather than deepening inequalities. The United Nations plays a central role in strengthening international cooperation to narrow these gaps, and we support efforts to advance its practical realization, including through a legally binding international instrument. Azerbaijan remains firmly committed to this objective. during our 2019-2023 chairmanship at the Non-Aligned Movement, with strengthened solidarity among developing countries, ensuring their perspectives shaped international decision-making and prioritizing the operationalization of the right to development. At the Human Rights Council in 2023, Azerbaijan led the facilitation of the HRC resolution on submitting the draft International Covenant on the right to development to the General Assembly. We continue our sponsorship and support through voluntary contributions to the OHCHR. On climate action, Azerbaijan's COP29 presidency placed climate finance and support for developing countries at the center of global efforts. Having evolved from a beneficiary country to a provider of humanitarian and development assistance, we share resources, expertise, and innovative solutions, such as public service delivery models with partner nations. Looking ahead, we must move from reaffirming the right to development to delivering real progress. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Azerbaijan. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Ethiopia.

Madam Chairperson, my delegation would like to extend its appreciation to the President of the General Assembly for convening this high-level meeting to commemorate the 40th anniversary of the Declaration on the Right to Development. My delegation aligns itself with the statements delivered by the Republic of Uganda on behalf of the Non-Aligned Movement and the Republic of Burundi on behalf of the African group, respectively. Since the adoption of the Declaration in 1986, several studies and reports have been issued by mandate holders and experts with a view to offer a comprehensive appraisal of progress, persistent gaps and emerging challenges in the realization of the right to development. Despite this right being clear in both substantive and procedural matter, the path to translating the declaration into binding international instrument took four decades. This raises legitimate concerns by developing countries when these commitments are delayed. The right to development as a fundamental human and people's right is deeply rooted in the African history. and development trajectory. In the same vein, in Ethiopia, our constitution clearly recognizes the right to development as enshrined in both the Declaration and the Banjul Charter. Our policies and strategies are human-centered and implemented with strong vigor to respond to the needs of the people. The OPE also underscores the need to rectify global structural inequalities and the need for meaningful participation of the global south in international economic governance. We also call on the international community to strengthen genuine international cooperation and provisional financing for development. The right to development is a fundamental human right by virtue of which every human being is entitled to participate in, contribute to, and enjoy economic, social, cultural, and political development. That's why the Declaration and the Draft Covenant on the Right to Development give emphasis to the integration of development and human rights. My delegation would like to reiterate its commitment to work with all member states and the mandate holders towards the realization of this fundamental right.

I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Ethiopia. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Ireland.

Madam Chairperson, dear friends, since the adoption of the Declaration 40 years ago, we have made remarkable progress. The number of people living in extreme poverty has fallen from 2.6 billion to 826 million. The under-five mortality rate has dropped to half its 2000 level. For the last 25 years, we have seen HIV/AIDS infection rates dropping. Yet today, those gains are under threat, particularly for those already furthest behind. The challenge before us is how we respond so as to leave no one behind. We are confronted with escalating food crises driven by conflict and climate change, and the impending super El Nino event, which could push at least 49 million additional people into acute food insecurity by the end of 2027. The alarm bells should be sounding as we witness democratic backsliding and waning attention to governance across the world, as well as an unprecedented pushback against human rights, including gender equality, sexual and reproductive health and rights, and the rights of LGBTQI+ peoples. The right to development cannot be realised without all human rights, which are universal, indivisible and mutually reinforcing. They must remain at the centre of our efforts and should never be subordinated to short-term political or economic considerations. An effective multilateral system has never been more needed. Yet, at that very moment we need it most, we are witnessing a retreat from the collective action that made the progress of the last decades possible. If we are to change course, we must renew and strengthen multilateral cooperation. That means making difficult choices and challenging established practices. We will shape the future of the international system, or will we allow financial pressures and short-term decisions to shape it for us? Our answer will have profound implications for the trajectory of global development in decades ahead. Our benchmark for success should be simple: are we delivering for those furthest behind? Addressing the enduring challenge of poverty remains essential. Without a clear focus on poverty, development efforts cementing inequality, instability and insecurity. The Declaration on the Right to Development remains as relevant as ever. It reminds us that development is fundamentally about people, their dignity, their rights and their ability to participate in the decisions that shape their lives. Therefore, we must recommit to make this declaration a living document, one that is relatable and accessible to all. The challenges, Chair, before us are immense, but so too is our collective capacity to address them. Thank you very much, Coimhheadh na dGaelach.
I thank the distinguished representative of Ireland. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Kuwait.

Sayid al-Rais.

Madam Chair, Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, it is our pleasure to take part in this commemorative high-level meeting on the occasion of the adoption of the Declaration on the Right to Development, representing an important juncture in international affairs and reaffirming development as a basic right of all people everywhere, and a steadfast affirmation of these rights. The right to development is a comprehensive and international right that is inalienable and that is interlinked with all human rights. Man is the focus of development, the first participant, and the most beneficiary. We stress the importance of continuing efforts of reforming the international financial structure to make it more equitable and more accessible to developing nations, enabling them to achieve strong economic development in a comprehensive and equitable manner, promoting opportunities for investment and creating employment opportunities, thus combating poverty. Four, decades after the adoption of the declaration, the challenge is no longer another reaffirmation of the right, rather it's operationalization in a manner that makes development a reality for people, and so that all peoples have a fair opportunity to contribute to, participate in, and benefit from development. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Kuwait. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Malaysia.

Madam President, 40 years ago, this Assembly affirmed that development is a right, not a privilege. The Declaration on the Right to Development places the human person at the centre of development. Development is not merely to benefit from progress, but to participate in, contribute to, and shape it. Nevertheless, four decades later, that promise remains under-delivered. Despite the remarkable economic and technological advances, advancement between developed and developing countries remain uneven, and inequality in wealth continues to grow. Conflict, climate change, debt vulnerabilities, and widening digital divides continue to constrain millions in developing countries. Malaysia has also sought to advance this agenda regionally. During our ASEAN chairmanship in 2025, ASEAN leaders adopted the ASEAN Declaration on promoting the right to development and the right to peace towards realising inclusive and sustainable development. Malaysia remains committed to multilateral cooperation and international solidarity. We will continue to engage constructively on the draft International Covenant on the Right to Development with a view to its subsequent adoption. As we commemorate 40 years of this declaration, our task now must work towards its realization and implementation. 40 years from now, history should not be judged by this declaration, excuse me, 40 years from now, history should not judge this declaration merely by the commitments we reaffirm, but by the lives we transform. Malaysia stands ready to work with all member states to make that promise a reality. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Malaysia. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Lao People's Democratic Republic.

Madam President, for four decades, the Declaration on the Right to Development has provided an important framework for advancing development as an integral part of human rights. Its central message remains highly relevant today. Development is a comprehensive economic, social, cultural, and political process. in which the human person is the central subject, active participant, and beneficiary of development. The La Paz Charter attaches great importance to the realization of the right to development. This principle is reflected in our national development policies, which place the people and their well-being at the center of the development process. In this regard, the government has continued to pursue policies aimed at promoting sustainable and inclusive economic growth, reducing poverty, improving livelihoods, and narrowing development gaps. Particular attention has been given to the improving access to quality education and healthcare, strengthening social protection, creating employment opportunities, developing infrastructure, and enhancing connectivity, especially for people living in rural and remote areas. We also continue to promote the participation of all segments of society in the development process, including women, children, persons with disabilities, and other vulnerable groups, while working to ensure that the benefits of development are shared broadly and equitably. These priorities are being further advanced through our national development plans in alignment with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. with the objective of building a more sustainable, inclusive and resilient economy and improving the quality of life of our people. The declaration also reminds us that national efforts must be complemented by an enabling international environment and effective international cooperation for developing countries, strengthen partnerships, adequate development financing, capacity building and access to technology remain important means for realizing the right to development and achieving the Sustainable Development Goals. In conclusion, the Lao PDR reaffirms its commitment to the principles and objectives of the Declaration. We will continue to translate these objectives and principles into our national development policies and concrete actions with the well-being of our people at the center by working with the international community towards a more equitable, inclusive, and sustainable future for all. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Lao People's Democratic Republic. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Congo.

Madam President, Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen, At the outset, I would like to use this opportunity to pay a solemn tribute to Mr. Denis Sassou Nguesso, President of the Republic of the Congo, who, in his vision, makes the right to development an inalienable sovereign right, a matter of dignity. 40 years after we adopted this historic declaration, we must speak about it in a clear-sighted fashion. For many nations, the right to development is a far-off prospect. We've seen deepening inequality, tighter budgets, and unsustainable debt levels. Propelled by President Nussengisso, We would like to remind everyone that the right to development is not a legal abstract notion. It is a political, economic, and moral imperative. The Republic of the Congo is fully shouldering its responsibility as it seeks to fight climate change. In the Congo Basin, we are protecting one of the planet's biggest carbon sinks. This is a strategic choice. promoted by our President, and it lies at the heart of the right to development. No country can develop if we are to live on a degraded planet, and no country should be penalized for protecting its environmental heritage, which belongs to all of humanity. The Congo calls for debt cancellation to give a real chance to the SDGs so that we can see structured economic reform, and solidarity with other nations. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Congo. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Saudi Arabia.

Saeed Al Raisi.

Madam Chairperson, ladies and gentlemen, we participate in the 40th anniversary on the Declaration of the Right to Development. recalling the importance of this right, enabling men to benefit from economic and social development, as well as other means that promote fundamental rights and dignity. We believe that comprehensive and sustainable development is based on making men the focus of development work. enabling societies and including everyone in enjoying the benefits of development. At the national level, that right has become a legal obligation with a view to achieving economic and social development in a fair and equitable manner. We have taken many measures in this regard, including our Vision 2030, which encompasses reforms and developments at all levels, legislative, institutional, judicial, and administrative. They have also included the provision of social protection, the promotion of small and midsize businesses, developing the employment market, and expanding women's participation. Through our cooperation with the United Nations organizations, including the UNDP and the UNHCR, we make further efforts to establish an uninterruptible link between the right to development and all other rights and sustainable development objectives as well. Our commitment to this right is not confined to our national borders. Through our Saudi Development Fund, we have participated and assisted in many different vital fields such as education, health, water, energy, transport, and agriculture in other countries. Since the beginning of its activities in 1975, the Fund has provided 813 development loans to 102 countries with a view in a total of $22.5 billion. After four decades of adopting the declaration, The path to development must be done through our total solidarity and support. Thank you.
I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Eritrea.

Mr. President, Excellencies, Today, gathering offers an opportunity to reaffirm our commitment and reflect on our collective progress. More importantly, to confront the structural inequalities that continue to hinder the realization of this inalienable right. Over the past decades, advances in science and technology have held immense potential to bridge the development gap. Yet these opportunities remain concentrated in the hands of a few, while many developing nations remain excluded. This digital and structural divide is a feature of the current global economic structure, architecture, which continues to reflect structural imbalances that penalize developing nations. Unfair trade barriers, arbitrary financial restrictions, unsustainable debt burdens, and unilateral coercive measures make it difficult for Global South developing nations to choose independent policies that best suit their own needs. Instead, they are forced to follow rules designed by wealthier nations. Eritrea reiterates its firm position that TMS are incompatible with the United Nations Charter and violate the fundamental right of peoples to determine their own socioeconomic paths. Mr. President, to accelerate the realization of the right to development and to build a just and sustainable future, I wish to highlight the following points. One, respecting the right of states to chart independent political and development policies. Two, eliminating unilateral course of measures that restrict access to resources, technology, and the international markets. Three, restructuring multilateral financial and economic institutions to ensure genuine representation and fair rules for developing countries. Four, supporting the elaboration and adoption of a legally binding instrument on the right to development to impose accountability and concrete international obligations.
I thank the distinguished representative of Eritrea. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Iraq.

Thank you, Madam President. We'd like to express our appreciation for the holding of this high-level segment on the 40th occasion of the adoption of the Declaration on the Right to Development. 40 years after it was adopted, it continues to reaffirm that the right to development is a human right and that every person and every people have the right to participate in, contribute to, and benefit from development. We believe that development is not confined to economic development. It is rather a comprehensive process based on social justice, equity, respect for human dignity, and all other human rights. We also believe that peace and development are interlinked. There can be no sustainable development without security and stability. My country, Iraq, has faced immense challenges due to terrorism, armed conflict, displacement, destruction of the infrastructure, as well as the increasing effects of climate change. Nevertheless, We continue our efforts to rehabilitate the affected areas, diversify the economy, provide employment opportunities, and promote the participation of women in development. And we would like to reiterate that our national efforts deserve genuine international support. Developing countries need an equitable opportunity to have access to financing, technology, capacity building and access to international markets. Also, the international financial structure needs to provide further opportunity for their participation in a manner that is more just. We are facing other serious challenges, such as the scarcity of water, the desertification, the shrinking of arable lands, and increasing temperatures, all requiring the promotion of international cooperation, the upholding of pledges regarding climate financing, as well as bearing common responsibilities even when they are not equal. On this occasion, we would like to reiterate our commitment to transform the principles of the declaration into reality and call upon all international parties in a transparent and constructive manner to promote the international legal framework of that right. And we will continue to cooperate with member states and the United Nations with a view to making the right to development a reality for all peoples without distinction and without leaving anyone behind.
I thank the distinguished representative of Iraq. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Turkey.

Thank you, Chair, distinguished delegates. Turkey welcomes this high-level segment commemorating the 40th anniversary of the Declaration on the Right to Development. Forty years ago, the international community affirmed that development is an inalienable human right. This vision remains as relevant today, as it reminds us that economic growth must be accompanied by social justice. that technological progress must serve human dignity and that the national development priorities must be supported by an enabling international environment. Turkey's own experience illustrates the value of sustained people-centered development. Over the past decades, we have made substantial progress in reducing poverty, expanding access to health and education, and empowering women. We share this experience in a spirit of partnership, but at the same time recognizing that each country must pursue its own development pathway. Yet, development cannot be sustained without peace. When there is war and conflict, we not only suffer humanitarian losses, we also witness the destruction of the whole foundation of development. Excellencies, Turkey attaches particular importance to development challenges of the LDCs. We have consistently supported the development priorities of LDCs, including through our financial contributions to the UN Technology Bank for LDCs, our engagement in South-South cooperation, and our support for initiatives that strengthen access to science, technology, and innovation. We believe that the 40th anniversary is an opportunity to reaffirm that development is a right, not a privilege. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Turkey. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Peru.

Thank you, Madam President. Four decades after the adoption of the Declaration on the Right to Development, Peru wishes to state once again that development should be to the service of the dignity and welfare of all people and communities, and particularly those who are most vulnerable. The commemoration today is of particular importance for my country. We played an active part in drawing up the declaration as a member of the group of government experts dealing with it. As we recall our contribution, we emphasize that the real enjoyment of human rights requires, apart from their recognition, material conditions, institutional capacities, and government policies which make these rights reality. Therefore, development must show in the form of tangible improvements in people's lives, high quality education, accessible health services, social infrastructure, access to basic services, and opportunities for decent jobs. These are elements which are essential in order to ensure opportunities for citizens. Nationally, Peru is committed to strengthening its institutions to transparency, accountability, and also to the efficient use of public resources. This means also that there has to be active participation, which is free and meaningful participation of people in decisions which affect their development. Peru sees development as part and parcel of the greater framework of human rights law. Therefore, it is vital that promoting this contributes to achieving all human rights and fundamental freedoms, consistently with international obligations entered into by States, including those pertaining to civil and political rights. Peru states that we have an unwavering commitment to inclusive, sustainable development, which is people-based. We also appeal for strengthening international cooperation so that the hope enshrined in the declaration becomes reality for our societies, which can prosper without leaving anyone behind. Thank you.
I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Maldives.

Ms. Milahir Rahman Ibrahim. President, Excellencies, distinguished guests. 40 years after the declaration, the right to development has a clear meaning for the Maldives. Every country should have the freedom and capacity to shape its future. The ambition of the Maldives is equally clear. President Dr. Mohamed Muizz has set goals for the country to become a developed country by 2040. Achieving that goal requires sustained investment in our people, communities, infrastructure, and institutions. For the Maldives, resilience begins with investment. In practice, this means stronger schools and hospitals, adequate housing, reliable infrastructure, renewable energy, digital capacity, and new opportunities for our people. These investments will strengthen communities and give individuals greater security, opportunity, while increasing our national capacity to determine our own development path. Yet countries can only make these choices when they have the financial space to invest. Development finance is becoming harder to access and increasingly expensive. High borrowing costs and debt repayments reduce the resources available for education, health, infrastructure, and other investments. that directly improve people's lives. This is where international cooperation matters. Finance must become accessible, adequate, and affordable. The civil law commitment should be implemented, particularly its commitments on debt sustainability, concession of finance, and reform of the international financial architecture. Climate finance must become simpler and faster to access, especially for adaptation. The Antigua and Barbuda agenda for SIDS gives us another part of answer. Development cooperation must strengthen national institutions, expand domestic capacity and support solutions determined by the countries themselves. 40 years ago, the declaration recognized a right to belonging to every person. Today, our responsibility is to create the conditions in which people and countries can exercise the right. For the Maldives, that means having the space, capacity and finance to invest in our own future. That is how we build resilience. That is how we develop Delhi for development. I thank you. Wassalamu alaikum warahmatullahi wabarakatuh.

Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Maldives. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Portugal.

Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, the year 2026 marks two pivotal milestones. the 14th anniversary of the Declaration on the Right to Development, and the 5th anniversary of the Constitution of the Portuguese Republic, which proudly enshrines this fundamental right. Portugal firmly grounds the right to development in the universal, indivisible, and interdependent nature of all human rights. Individuals are the ultimate right holders, states the primary duty bearers. guided by the principle of leaving no one behind, our commitment to multilateralism remains unwavering. Excellencies, the protection of all human rights, civil, cultural, economic, political and social, defines our core priorities, eradicating poverty, advancing gender equality, addressing the climate emergency and navigating the digital transition. Through our development cooperation strategy 2030, Portugal continues to accelerate the implementation of the Sustainable Development Goals. Our official development assistance maintains a steady upward trajectory, with a strong focus on Portuguese-speaking African countries and Timor-Leste, while expanding across the Ibero-American region and the Pacific. Ladies and gentlemen, we know that there is no lasting peace without development, no development without human rights, and no development without adequate funding. Portugal remains fully committed to the financing for development agenda. We are pioneering innovative mechanisms, such as debt for climate swaps with Cabo Verde and Sao Tome and Principe, and scaling up triangular cooperation through our dedicated Portugal-Latin America Africa Fund. Furthermore, capacity building is essential. In partnership with the United Nations, Portugal has launched fellowship programs spanning ocean governance, digital transformation, and outer space, empowering states and individuals to drive inclusive, multi-stakeholder decision-making. Excellencies, to give concrete form to our values, between 2023 and 2025, Portugal allocated over 40 million euro in direct contributions to UN agencies and programs. 40 years after the adoption of this landmark declaration, Portugal stands ready to work with all partners to ensure that development ceases to be a privilege for the few and becomes a lived reality I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Portugal. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Palau.

President, Excellencies, 40 years after the adoption of the Declaration, perhaps the most important question is a simple one. What does the right to development actually mean in the lives of our people? In Palau, it means that a young person should be able to see a future and find opportunity at home. It means our people should have access to quality healthcare, education, and essential services, even when delivering them across a small island nation comes at a higher cost. And increasingly, it means ensuring that the development we have already achieved can withstand a changing climate. For Palau, this is a very real challenge. Our national planning includes relocating critical facilities, including our national hospital and vulnerable schools, away from areas exposed to climate risk, while strengthening water systems and other essential infrastructure. When a small country must use its limited resources not only to advance development, but also to protect what generations have already built, the right development takes a very practical meaning. But it is also about having a choice in that development. Development should not be simply measured by what we build. it should also be measured by whether our people can participate in shaping it, whether they benefit from it, and whether what we build can endure. For countries like Palau, however, national effort alone is not enough. Climate impacts, geographic isolation, limited capacity, and barriers to accessible development finance all affect how quickly, and in some cases, whether our ambitions can become reality. 40 years on, this is where the promise of the declaration must become practical. We reiterate that the sustainable development is something that requires building capacity and increasing the ability and resilience and dealing with crises and conflicts, so as to make the response collective among all states. Thank you, Madam President, Excellencies, distinguished delegates. The international community took a historic step 40 years ago by affirming that development is not merely an economic objective, nor is it a privilege for some. The adoption of the UN Declaration on the Right to Development in 1986 established a fundamental principle. Every human being and all peoples have the right to participate in, contribute to, and benefit from development. Forty years later, we are not gathered here merely to commemorate that achievement. We have to rather ask a fundamental question. Have we created the necessary international conditions for the right to development to become a reality for all? Excellencies, the issue of unilateral coercive measures is an undeniable case in point. Such measures can restrict access to financial resources, equipment, investment, scientific knowledge and advanced technologies. For developing countries, however, the consequences can extend far beyond the immediate political dispute. The loss of access to technology today may mean the loss of productive capacity, scientific expertise and development opportunities tomorrow. Excellencies, the right to development cannot be realized without the protection of fundamental rights to life and health. The absolutely unlawful war waged by the Zionist and US regimes against the Islamic Republic of Iran has demonstrated the devastating consequences that attacks on civilians and health infrastructure can have on these rights. Medical and emergency facilities, hospitals, ambulances, pharmaceutical and vaccine production facilities, medical research institutions, and humanitarian personnel have all been severely damaged and attacked. Such unlawful military aggression has continued by the US naval blockade, together with disruptions to essential health and pharmaceutical supply chains, not only caused immediate loss of life and human suffering, but also undermined the long-term capacity of a country to provide essential health care, produce medicines, retain specialized human capital, and protect the health of its population, particularly groups with special needs. The same pattern of destruction inflicted upon my country extends beyond health infrastructure to schools, universities, scientific and research institutions, cultural heritage, media organization, and sport facilities, with serious implications for the enjoyment of economic, social, and cultural rights. These consequences demonstrate that the protection and realization of the right to development cannot be achieved without holding accountable those who violate the very essence of development through belligerence, wars, and occupation. Thank you, Madam.

Thank you, Madam President, Your Excellencies, distinguished delegates. Costa Rica joins in this commemoration of the 40th anniversary of the Declaration on the Right to Development. We believe that its main principle is still entirely relevant. Everybody should be able to play an active part in development, contribute to it and benefit from its results. 40 years on, challenge is still to ensure that this principle becomes real opportunities for all. Our experience in Costa Rica has shown us that development depends on sustained public decisions, investment in health, education, protection, social protection, extending the opportunities for our people. Here we need able institutions, resources and opportunities. If we we look at the lack of biodiversity, climate change, pollution, we see these affecting living conditions and the possibilities development. AI digitalization can open opportunities, provided that we look at the gulfs and access the abilities of humans. We need a a full image of our country. When we look at development, figures can obscure problems when it comes to public financing, adaptation to climate change, and protection of the biodiversity. Costa Rica believes that international cooperation must deal with real needs. We need access to knowledge, to technology. as well as funding which enables countries to invest in their priorities for sustainable development. Madam, observing the declaration means that people can study, have healthcare, have dignified work, flourish in a clean and healthy as well as a sustainable environment. The right to development is there when these opportunities are available to everybody. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Costa Rica. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Holy See.

Madam President, the Holy See welcomes today high level meeting to commemorate the 40th anniversary of the Declaration on the Right to Development. This declaration identifies the individual person as the focus and beneficiary of the right to development, with the state as the primary duty bearer. It also explicitly connects this right to the obligation of international cooperation to support states in their duties as their primary promoters and protectors of the individual's right to development. The right to development is rooted in the God-given dignity of each person, from conception to natural death, regardless of age, nationality, race, religion, ethnicity, sex, or disability. Article 14 emphasizes that for individuals as well as for nations, development is both a duty and a right. Minimum conditions are required for enabling every person and people to flourish in accord with their dignity without being kept in a state of dependence or excluded from access to necessary goods. 40 years after the adoption of the declaration, These minimum conditions remain out of reach for too many. Poverty, food insecurity, conflict, climate change, and debt burdens are among the obstacles that hinder the exercise of the right to development. This right is realized through renewed and concrete action and international cooperation guided by solidarity and the recognition of the shared responsibility. States, particularly those facing the greatest structural challenges, should have access to the financial, technological, and human resources necessary to advance the development of their peoples. Such cooperation should empower women and men to become the true protagonists of their own development. Madam President, today's commemoration provides a timely opportunity to reaffirm the commitment to a genuine human development rooted in dignity, sustained by solidarity, and then the flourishing of every person.

Thank you.

Madam President, as we commemorate the 40th anniversary of the United Nations Declaration on the Right to Development, 40 years on, we are challenged to rethink how we measure progress, not by economic growth alone, but by whether people are able to shape, contribute to, and benefit from development in dignity and on an equal basis. It reminds us that development is inseparable from human rights, that freedom must be matched by opportunity, and that national responsibility must be reinforced by international solidarity. Indeed, before the world adopted the declaration, Africa had already translated the right to development into binding regional law. In 1981, the OAU, predecessor of the African Union, adopted the African Charter on Human and People's Rights. The charter entered into force on 21 October 1986, and Article 22 gave the right to development a binding regional legal expression. The jurisprudence of African human rights mechanisms It subsequently affirmed the practical meaning of this right. Development must be pursued with communities through participation, consultation, inclusion, and equitable benefit sharing. Today, the right to development provides a unifying framework for responding to some of the defining challenges of our time, conflict, climate shocks, debt distress, inequality, and digital exclusion. Agenda 2063 and the UN 2030 Agenda provide complementary pathways for translating this vision into measurable progress. The African Union's 2026 theme further reminds us that water and sanitation are not merely development sectors. They are enablers of health, education, gender equality, livelihood, resilience, and peace. Through the joint AU-UN human rights framework, the AU's high-level dialogue and steering committee are also strengthening early warning, national human rights institutions, business and human rights, and human rights compliance in peace operations. Looking ahead, digital transformation, artificial intelligence, and just transition to profoundly shape development. But technology cannot become a new source of exclusion. These transformations must be governed by equality, participation, transparency, and accountability. Our priorities must therefore include affordable and meaningful connectivity, digital skills, strong data protection, human rights impact assessments, African innovation, and the fair sharing of technological benefits. A robust international covenant on the right to development can help clarify responsibilities and strengthen common standards.

Thank you, Madam President. It gives me pleasure to participate with you in this 40th anniversary of the adoption of the Declaration on the Right to Development. We consider development a basic cornerstone of peace and stability. Our Vision 2045 provides a framework for that concept towards an Arab region that is more prosperous and innovative. However, to speak of development in our region cannot be separated from the reality of occupation and armed conflict. There is no clearer example than the Palestinian people. We cannot speak of development while this people is denied its right to self-determination, whose life is being destroyed, and who is denied sovereignty on its land and resources. The right of the Palestinian people to development is part and parcel of its right to self-determination and the establishment of its independent state. 40 years after the adoption of the declaration, it is not only required to reaffirm that right, however, to find the means to make it a reality, to enhance hope amongst people and aspiration to a better future as a regional and international responsibility on us all. Thank you.
